summary: Describes the common ways that Voice over IP providers connect to each other using SIP peering. It sorts them into static and on-demand setups, and further into direct and indirect ones. The examples are not exhaustive, and this document is informational.

eli5.summary: Two phone companies can be connected by a permanent private line or by finding each other only when a call comes. This document draws out the common ways that happens for internet phone calls.

subtitle: Describes how Voice over IP providers peer and exchange calls using SIP, covering fixed relationships and dynamic discovery.

tldr.problem: Voice over IP providers need standard ways to interconnect and exchange calls. Different business and technical scenarios require different peering approaches, and implementers need clear examples of each.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC categorizes SIP peering into two types: static peering (fixed relationships set up in advance) and on-demand peering (dynamically discovering peers when calls arrive). Each type can be direct (peer-to-peer) or indirect (using intermediate providers). The document provides concrete use cases and message flows showing how each works.
tldr.outcome: This RFC provided reference implementations and architecture guidance for the SPEERMINT working group's standards. It helped establish a common vocabulary for VoIP interconnection and showed that the existing SIP protocol could support multiple peering models.

today: RFC 6405 remains the canonical reference for VoIP peering models. While the specific technologies continue to evolve (DNS SRV, ENUM, DNSSEC), the fundamental architecture and use case categories described here are still accurate and widely deployed in modern VoIP networks.

sections.title: VoIP Interconnection Models
sections.content:
The growth of internet-based voice calling requires a way for different Voice over IP service providers to exchange calls. SIP peering is the standard approach: two providers use the Session Initiation Protocol to negotiate and set up calls for each other's customers.

This RFC catalogues the most common use cases for SIP peering as of 2011. These cases show different scenarios that arise from business relationships (static versus dynamic) and network topology (direct versus using intermediaries). Rather than being exhaustive, the document captures the major patterns deployed or proposed at the time.

Understanding these use cases is important for SPEERMINT (Session PEERing for Multimedia INTerconnect), an IETF framework that develops standards and requirements for this interconnection.
sections.eli5: Internet phone companies need to connect and send calls to each other. There are several common ways to do this.

sections.title: SPEERMINT Architecture Components
sections.content:
The RFC uses a standard architecture model with key roles. The Originating SSP (Service Provider) is the provider from which a call originates. The Terminating SSP is where the call is delivered. In many cases, intermediate systems are involved.

Within each SSP domain, there are several functions. The Lookup Function (LUF) translates a phone number into routing information. The Location Routing Function (LRF) determines which server handles that information. The Signaling Path Border Element (SBE) is the gateway that exchanges SIP messages with peer providers. The Data Path Border Element (DBE) handles the actual voice stream.

In indirect peering scenarios, there may be an Indirect SSP providing intermediate services, or Assisting LUF/LRF providers that offer lookup and routing services to multiple SSPs.
sections.eli5: Each phone company has lookup systems to find customers, border computers to talk to other companies, and lines to carry the actual voice.

sections.title: Static Peering: Pre-Arranged Connections
sections.content:
Static peering describes a relationship where two service providers establish their connection before any calls are exchanged. They agree in advance on technical parameters like IP addresses, transport protocols, maximum call rates, and authentication methods. This approach is used when both providers want consistent, tightly controlled connections.

Static direct peering is the simplest form: two SSPs connect directly peer-to-peer. The originating SSP uses its own lookup and routing functions to identify that a call should be sent to the peer provider, and routes it directly using a pre-configured address. This model is common when two providers have a business relationship and want full control of the connection.

Static indirect peering uses intermediate providers. The originating SSP may use an assisting lookup provider to determine where to route the call, or it may use an intermediate SSP that provides peering services to multiple smaller providers. This model is useful for smaller providers that cannot afford direct connections to many peers, or for specialized routing scenarios.
sections.eli5: Two companies can agree ahead of time how to connect and stay connected. Or smaller companies can use a middleman to reach many others without having many separate agreements.

sections.title: On-Demand Peering: Dynamic Discovery
sections.content:
On-demand peering takes a different approach: providers discover each other dynamically when calls arrive, rather than establishing connections in advance. When a call comes in for an unknown destination, the originating provider's lookup function queries DNS or other services to discover the terminating provider's address. The connection is established just for that call.

This model is more scalable because providers need not maintain permanent connections to every possible peer. However, it introduces complexity: the discovery mechanism must be reliable, security is harder to control, and call setup is slightly slower. On-demand peering is useful in scenarios with many potential peers, such as internet-wide voice services or specialized call routing where the set of peers changes frequently.

Both static and on-demand models can use direct connections or route through intermediaries, depending on the providers' network topology and peering policies.
sections.eli5: Instead of a permanent line, companies can look up each other when needed. This is slower to connect but means fewer permanent connections.

sections.title: Call Flow: How SIP Peering Works
sections.content:
The RFC illustrates each use case with detailed message flows showing how SIP works in practice. In all scenarios, the flow follows similar steps: the originating SSP receives a call, looks up the destination, determines the next hop (either a direct peer or intermediate service), and sends a SIP INVITE request toward the terminating SSP.

The INVITE travels via any intermediaries, with each system adding routing information. The INVITE includes the originating user's identity, the destination (usually a phone number), and various SIP parameters. The terminating SSP receives the INVITE, validates the caller, and routes it to the destination user.

Media (voice) typically flows along a different path than signaling, using RTP. The signaling path defines which SBEs are involved; the media path determines how the voice stream is routed. Complex interconnections may involve several intermediaries on the signaling path and separate media gateways.

Each use case shows different instantiations of these basic elements: static direct has the simplest message flow, while on-demand scenarios show more complex routing and lookups.
sections.eli5: A call travels step by step through the networks. Each company knows what the next step is, either because they agreed in advance or because they looked it up.
